articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls more than 2%, extending slide to third day as Nvidia drags down AI trade: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls more than 2%, extending slide to third day as Nvidia drags down AI trade: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Monday, dragged down by key technology stocks, as traders reacted to more developments surrounding Nvidia .
The Nasdaq Composite declined 2.49% to end at 24,509.76, while the S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 739.38 points, or 1.41%, closing at 51,608.17.
Shares of Nvidia were down 4.1%. The pressure came as a source familiar with the matter told CNBC that the chipmaker's board of directors is not discussing bringing back Jensen Huang as its chief executive.
Adding to the pressure, the Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese firms rent Nvidia's computing power located in other countries. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the weekend also called for a " dramatic shakeup " at the company, urging its board to look outside the company for its next CEO.
"Two weeks ago investing in this name looked like a safe journey down a well-lit long hallway," said Mike Mussio, chief investment officer at FBB Capital Partners. Now, he added, "there are several dark corners that people feel they need to peek around to glean additional information before moving forward."
"There is plenty to digest, and many jumpy investors seem unwilling to stick around for answers," Mussio continued.
The embattled chipmaker is preparing to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Huang's exit as CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"Strong results won't resolve the questions surrounding Jensen's departure," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "For a company that spent 33 years under one CEO, this is about more than beating expectations. Nvidia now needs to show that the business can continue delivering without the man who built it."
Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade were under pressure along with Nvidia. Fellow chipmakers Micron Technology and Intel lost more than 7%, while Advanced Micro Devices declined 5%. Memory chip name Sandisk pulled back about 8%. Additionally, shares of computer maker Dell Technologies also declined almost 7%, while software stock Oracle moved down about 5%.
The sell-off broadened beyond just AI-linked names as the session went on, with selling pressure picking up in areas like financials. In that group, Morgan Stanley , Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase shed more than 2%.
Another key test for the trade this week is Anthropic's initial public offering . The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.49% to end at 24,509.76, and the S&P 500 lost 1.92% to settle at 7,416.59. It was the third consecutive losing day for both indexes.
The Dow Industrials declined 739.38 points, or 1.41%, to 51,608.17.
Michael Burry of "Big Short" fame is retaining his bearish bets on Nvidia ahead of Tuesday's earnings, as well as those on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF , insurance company MetLife and military technology firm Palantir , according to a Monday blog post.
He said he has a "large position" in put options linked to those asset.
Burry closed out of puts in other parts of the equities market, including one hyperscaler that is central to the future of the super intelligence buildout, on volatility concerns.
"I closed out of the Oracle ( ORCL ) puts, and I also closed out of the last bit of my Caterpillar( CAT ) puts on the continued downward volatility in those names," he said.
The VIX volatility index, a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, jumped as much as 25% Monday to a session high of 24.05.
That left the VIX at the highest in a week, since it reached 25.08 on Nov. 9, and was the largest percentage gain since the VIX soared almost 60% on Nov. 5.
The VIX is now on track to rise for a third consecutive day for the firs time since Nov. 2.
The S&P 500 was down nearly 2% on Monday, and all sectors linked to the index except for one suffered losses.
The consumer staples sector was higher by 0.3% in afternoon trading. Conversely, every other S&P 500 sector fell, with information technology and communication services taking the lead on that front. Those two were down 2.7% and 2.6%, respectively.
Consumer discretionary and energy were also key laggards, with the former falling 2.2% and the latter down 2%.
Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on a investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, the person said. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or Nvidia secrets.
Read the full story here .
— Seema Mody and Kif Leswing
Northcoast Research downgraded Costco Wholesale to neutral from buy on Monday after the stock's run higher this year.
The wholesale club has shown "remarkable success" as inflation drove shoppers into its stores, analyst Chuck Cerankosky said. However, shares currently trade at 48.4 times earnings.
"At multiples comparable to those of tech stocks and the rate at which the company is growing earnings, we believe shares of Costco Wholesale are valued fairly," he wrote in a note to clients.
The stock, which has gained 29% year to date, hit a 52-week high on Monday.
Despite uncertainty about the future of chipmaker Nvidia's leadership, there's strength ahead for semiconductors, according to Trivariate Research.
The firm expects "strong" earnings results from Nvidia this week and from memory maker Micron next month, supporting positive trends in returns over the next year.
"We think Semiconductors have a reasonable chance of being 50% higher in a year," Adam Parker at Trivariate wrote in a Sunday analysis.
Shares of Nvidia bounced on Thursday but failed to build on that progress on Friday, leading analysts at Wolfe to reconsider the $150 support level maintained last week.
"The stock successfully held that key $150 support level, after Thursday's notable intraday reversal. Unfortunately, the stock failed to build off of that reversal on Friday. Should price end up losing it, the next major support level sits around $100," Rob Ginsberg at Wolfe wrote in a Sunday note.
Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.
The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.
Read the full story here .
The three major averages kicked off the first trading session of the week in the red.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.4% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 declined 0.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 78 points, or 0.2%.
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive technology being exported to China .
Commerce's action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department, in a press release, said that the BIS rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council." Read more .

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.title_zh: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.content_orig:
A nationwide outage impacting Chase banking services Monday led some customers to report trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.
The outage began Monday morning, and it was unclear how long it would take to resolve, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The issues were affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The issues at Chase are the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence linking the incidents.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.
The problems at Chase were internal and caused by a technical bug, not a cyber issue, said a separate source who was also familiar with the situation.
The issues with Chase accounts appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds. An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
Kayla Steinberg is a producer at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders.
The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole allowing China to sidestep a ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. Chinese firms have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Whether to close the loophole has been a significant source of contention within the Trump administration.
The new rule is intended to make it harder for Chinese firms to remotely access the chips. It will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran.
Data centers are also required to perform strict checks on their customers to determine if they are linked to those countries. And the U.S. will now require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.
The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the administration said in a news release.
The plan to crack down on China’s ability to access the coveted A.I. chips comes as President Trump is scheduled to travel to Asia. He will travel to the Philippines and then to China for an economic summit, where he is expected to meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping and discuss the war in Iran, nuclear nonproliferation and trade. The data center rules could create a new source of friction between the countries, at a time when Mr. Trump has been trying to keep a fragile trade truce with China intact.

articles.title_orig: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.title_zh: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.content_orig:
More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue last fiscal year was generated by China – a massive cut that shows the size of the chip giant’s murky business with the US adversary, according to a report.
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang helped power an ecosystem in which it sold its most powerful chips to east Asian data centers that in turn powered tech offered by Chinese tech giants like Alibaba, according to reports.
Such deals drove more than a fifth of Nvidia’s revenue during the previous fiscal year, according to Culper Research, the short-selling firm that originally called out Nvidia’s China issues in May.
Huang’s efforts to supply China with key AI tech showered Nvidia with an eye-watering $12.4 billion in revenue in the six months through July 26 of this year, or 7% of its global revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal, which added that countless more billions of dollars could ultimately trace back to Chinese customers.
The dealings were a workaround to US export controls that sought to keep Nvidia’s top-of-the-line tech out of the hands of Chinese firms – and proved to be a cash cow for the chip giant, according to the Journal report .
As the full extent of Nvidia’s lucrative China business emerges, the Commerce Department announced Monday it is nixing the provision that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
Despite US export restrictions that have thwarted US chip sales directly to China, Nvidia sold chips to firms that set up data centers in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia which then sold the computing power to Chinese tech giants.
Some of those firms – including Singapore-based Megaspeed , which was led by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy and mistress to the former Nvidia CEO – have even been suspected of forwarding chips directly to China.
Between March 2024 and June 2025, Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips to companies in China, according to the WSJ report.
Shipment records show orders for several hundred thousand of the type of chips that US regulations intended to keep out of Chinese hands. The report notes that records don’t specify how many of the chips were actually delivered or where they originated from.
The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third-party countries, according to a Monday press release .
A license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion,” according to the new rule .
In a Sunday letter addressed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington – the top Dem on the Senate Commerce Committee – urged the Commerce secretary to reinforce export controls on the sale of AI chips to China.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote. “These companies are exploiting a loophole in US export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People’s Republic of China].
Nvidia says it works to prevent smuggling.
Megaspeed told the Journal that it conducts lawful business and designs its supply chain to comply with US export controls. Megaspeed added that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation.
Lutnick has come under fire since the revelations with critics on Capitol Hill questioning why the agency didn’t blacklist Megaspeed. Lutnick – whose job is speculated to be in jeopardy – is set to testify before the Senate about his agency’s handling of AI chip export controls.

articles.title_orig: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
articles.title_zh: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
articles.content_orig:
The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.
However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?
The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won’t launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA’s lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.
Given what is known publicly, and what Ars has heard privately, here are some educated guesses about all of this.
The first thing we can say for sure is that all estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt, including those in this article. Putting humans on any space vehicle is a difficult and time-consuming task, even outside of the requirements that NASA would impose for its astronauts.
The original target for launching humans on Starship (then known as the Interplanetary Transport System) set a decade ago was 2024. That was for a Mars mission. Then, in 2018 , SpaceX announced a lunar flyby mission on Starship with a target launch in 2023. This dearMoon mission was canceled in 2024. In 2022, SpaceX and Dennis Tito announced a lunar flyby mission later in the 2020s.
More recently, according to sources, SpaceX has been telling individuals interested in launching on Starship that it could begin offering flights by 2029. I probably would not put too much stock in this date.
All of this is to say, we cannot learn much from history other than to deeply discount any public launch dates on Starship for humans.
Most likely, the first humans to fly on Starship in space will do so after launching from Earth inside the NASA Orion spacecraft. Once in orbit they will then dock with Starship before transiting to the Moon, landing there in Starship, launching from the Moon back to Orion, and then returning to Earth inside NASA’s spacecraft.
NASA signed an agreement with SpaceX to develop Starship as this “Human Landing System” in 2021, with a lunar landing targeted for 2024. To no one’s surprise, this target has moved to 2028, and there remains considerable uncertainty about the viability of this date.
Nevertheless, the success of Saturday’s tower catch should help propel the Starship program toward a higher launch cadence, which is essential for lunar missions. It therefore seems plausible, but not certain, that humans could land on the Moon inside Starship before the end of this decade.
Again, how soon SpaceX achieves this target will depend upon its prioritization of a Human Landing System, among its other major goals to accomplish with Starship. At this point, SpaceX appears to be more focused on revenue-generating activities such as launching Starlink, and eventually, Starmind data center satellites.
Much has been made about the fact that Starship does not have a launch abort system—a feature of most human spacecraft that allows a crew vehicle to be rapidly pulled away from an exploding rocket.
This may not matter should SpaceX conduct its own human spaceflight missions. Unlike NASA, which imposes detailed human-rating requirements on vehicles carrying its astronauts, the Federal Aviation Administration does not certify commercial spacecraft as safe for passengers, instead operating under a regulatory framework that emphasizes informed consent and protection of the uninvolved public. Should SpaceX reach the point where it can launch Starship reliably, it will have the confidence it needs to press forward with human flights. Conceivably, this could happen within a few years.
According to potential customers, SpaceX is developing variants of the Human Landing System Starship for human flights, potentially carrying a few dozen people to the Moon. And such a prospect is tantalizing, for the interior of Starship’s pressurized cabin is almost unimaginably large for a spacecraft. A single Starship lunar lander has a pressurized habitable volume greater than the comparable volume of the International Space Station. This would be extraordinary.
Yet it is not a simple step to go from the current lunar lander design to an Earth lander. NASA’s lunar lander will never need to experience the tremendous heating of atmospheric reentry or perform the dramatic flip maneuver and propulsive landing that Starship uses to return home. Certifying those capabilities for human passengers, particularly on a vehicle without a traditional launch escape system, is an entirely different challenge.
Moreover, building a commercial human spaceflight business on Starship would be time-consuming and would likely not be nearly as profitable as launching Starlink satellites into space. And the risk is far greater—spaceflight remains dangerous, and the loss of a human crew would be a major negative for a publicly traded company. On the other hand, losing dozens of Starlink satellites on an errant launch would be a blip.
Despite Starship’s enormous theoretical capacity, SpaceX has also shown little interest in developing it as a crew transportation vehicle for commercial space stations in the near term. Several private space station operators have approached SpaceX about the possibility of Starship bringing astronauts to and from their stations. SpaceX indicated it was not interested.
Putting all of this together, I would not expect humans to land on Earth in Starship before 2030, and plausibly not until at least the mid-2030s.

articles.title_orig: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
articles.title_zh: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
articles.content_orig:
When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi , the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations.
But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said . Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months.
In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring.
“They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack.
The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine.
Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses.

articles.title_orig: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
articles.title_zh: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
articles.content_orig:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

articles.title_orig: US Moves to Curb Remote Access to Nvidia’s Advanced AI Chips
articles.title_zh: US Moves to Curb Remote Access to Nvidia’s Advanced AI Chips
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
The federal government is stepping up scrutiny of semiconductor exports to ensure that such shipments don't bypass existing regulations prohibiting their sale to certain U.S. competitors, such as China. The temporary regulations follow last week's shock resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company.
Huang's exit has heightened concerns that China and other nations could access Nvidia's advanced chips by renting computing resources through data centers in Southeast Asia.
"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday. "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security."
In addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the new rule will require licenses for exporting, re-exporting, or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. BIS said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
The interim rule notes that advances in cloud computing have made it easier for foreign nations to access American AI computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.
The Commerce Department wants to "ensure that computing power, based on U.S. technology located in foreign data centers, is not used in a manner contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests," the rule states.
The rule aims to align remote-access protections with existing controls governing physical access to sensitive American technology, the Commerce Department said.
Existing regulations on chip exports apply only to the most advanced semiconductors. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing," President Trump said in remarks at the White House on Monday.
Mr. Trump is heading to Asia on Monday, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Chinese officials have said the country was not involved in Huang's affair with the suspected spy.

articles.title_orig: Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres
articles.title_zh: Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres
articles.content_orig:
One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on Large Language Models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.
A new study has tallied up energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 in the United States. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference that could be tracked moving forward.
The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.
In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.
That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.
Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.
A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use.
The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straight-forward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO 2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use.
This yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO 2 emissions.
These data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear.
This doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence company, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time.
This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gas to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.)
Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature . The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.
When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.
Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.
This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.
Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.
Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’
You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring.
Bonta, at a press conference, cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face .
OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September.  rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry.
On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites."
"But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said.
Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law.
"OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said.
The attorney general said he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians."
"But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront."
Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models.
Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have since disclosed incidents where their own models went rogue. But OpenAI is the first to be sued in connection with such incidents by California.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri, in a statement on the lawsuit, said, "Since the Hugging Face incident, we've undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity."
"We've published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment," Pusateri said.
"This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," Pusateri said.
Bonta's lawsuit adds to OpenAI's growing list of legal woes.
In June, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users.
OpenAI is also facing lawsuits alleging that the company's ChatGPT platform led users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide.
California's lawsuit comes almost three months after a suit by Bonta and a coalition of other state attorneys general ended with Meta agreeing to pay $16.7 billion after being accused of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by its apps, including Facebook and Instagram. California could receive $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion from that agreement.
OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, setting the stage for a potentially massive initial public offering in 2027.
It is not clear how, if at all, Bonta's lawsuit will affect the IPO.
Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, said she had not closely followed news about the suit.
But Buyer, in an email, said, "Potential IPO buyers weigh a laundry list of risk factors, some more heavily than others."
"Investors generally do their best to assess timing and a continuum of potential outcomes," Buyer said. "Often, they will speak with uninvolved law firms in calculating the potential outcomes. Then, the risks, the timing and each investors' preferred holding period factor into the price they are willing to pay - assuming they have the option to buy or pass."
"Overall the aggregate belief about the risks — all risks — factor in to the IPO price," she said.

articles.title_orig: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.title_zh: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase reports an issue that appears to be causing outages to online and in-person banking services
An issue with Chase banking services led to some customers of that institution and others reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds Monday.
The issues appeared to be affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The issues at Chase were caused by a “technical bug, not a cyber issue,” according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
A Zelle representative said that a technical issue on its platform originated with Chase.
“This is a Chase issue,” a Zelle spokesman told NBC News. “You need to speak to them.”
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
The outages were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade .
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.content_orig:
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.﻿
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.﻿
Apple is working on a face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front-facing camera for authentication, and it’s already testing it with the new iOS 27.3 beta released today, as reported by MacRumors . Currently, the only way to unlock the iPhone Duo is by using Touch ID or entering a passcode, which might feel like a step back if you prefer face authentication using the Face ID feature available on other iPhones.
The iPhone Duo’s face unlock feature seemingly has a few caveats, however: it’s only available for the lock screen, you can only use your face for an unlock if you have used Touch ID or input a passcode within 45 minutes, and you can’t use the face authentication for Apple Pay purchases.
iOS 27.3 is set to launch publicly in December, Apple said last month , so should the feature make it to the full release, you may not have to wait too long for it to be officially available.
Apple reportedly wants to add Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo, Bloomberg reports .

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi, Putin to discuss ’world peace’, China says
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi, Putin to discuss ’world peace’, China says
articles.content_orig:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.
“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”
Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.
Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
after newsletter promotion
China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.
Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.
“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.
US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC .
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.
Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.content_orig:
In the past week, shares of Nvidia ( NVDA -3.96% ) have been in a downward spiral. News that Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO and has been involved in multiple affairs, one of which may involve a Chinese spy, has significantly weighed on the company's valuation.
The stock has fallen so sharply that it is now trading at levels it hasn't been at since June of last year. Given how sudden and significant the sell-off has been, many investors are likely worried that there may still be worse to come. Could the tech stock fall to $100?
Image source: Getty Images.
When things are going well for a stock, the temptation is to assume it'll only continue to do well and rise higher. And when things are going poorly, many investors may fear that things will only get worse. Both outlooks, however, can be incredibly irrational. Sooner or later, the excitement or panic fades, and the stock stabilizes and may even end up going in the opposite direction.
Due to its sharp decline, Nvidia's stock is now trading at around 20 times its trailing earnings. And on a forward basis, based on analyst expectations of future earnings, its forward price-to-earnings multiple is just ten. That's an incredibly low valuation given that the S&P 500 average is a forward earnings multiple of 19.
The stock is already heavily discounted , and for a more significant decline to take place, one that takes it to $100, that would likely require there to be much more negative news around the tech business. And there would also likely need to be an all-out crash in the tech sector.
NASDAQ · As of 2:56 PM ET 11/16/26
The last time Nvidia's stock was at around $100 was after the Liberation Day tariffs were announced in April 2025. Global trade uncertainty weighed on not only Nvidia but the markets as a whole, and unless there's that kind of uncertainty and fear rattling the markets once more, I wouldn't expect Nvidia to fall to those levels anytime soon.
Nvidia is already an incredibly cheap-looking stock to buy given how well it has performed in recent years. Waiting for an even lower price could be risky for investors, because the risk is that it may never reach those levels; buying the stock now may be a much better move than holding out hope that it will fall even further.

articles.title_orig: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.title_zh: Warsh Says Fed Is Gaming Out How AI Could Reshape Economy
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Le Pen says France will keep giving Ukraine aid if she is elected
articles.title_zh: Le Pen says France will keep giving Ukraine aid if she is elected
articles.content_orig:
European leaders need urgently to prepare for a far-right French president who would cut off Kyiv’s financial lifeline
E urope is consumed by two debates that matter less than it thinks, while neglecting one that matters enormously. The first is who should represent the EU in negotiations with Russia. This is largely irrelevant because there is little prospect of serious Ukraine peace talks before the end of winter - despite the fanfare that has surrounded discussions in Abu Dhabi this week. Russia has powerful incentives to escalate the war over the coming months in an attempt to break Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale.
The second is Donald Trump’s approach to Ukraine. This matters less than it once did – and not only because he is now more constrained by a Democratic Congress. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has provided no new US military aid to Kyiv. American weapons sales remain important to Ukraine’s war effort, but Trump’s military interventions in the Middle East have further strained supplies of the weapons Ukraine needs most – notably Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine does remain heavily dependent on US early warning intelligence , particularly to detect incoming Russian ballistic missiles, a capability Europe is unlikely to replicate fully before 2030. But the broader point stands: the US is a less indispensable partner to Ukraine than it was two years ago.
The debate European leaders are neglecting is much closer to home: what happens if Marine Le Pen wins France’s presidential election in six month’s time?
A president Le Pen would suspend France’s bilateral aid to Ukraine. More consequentially, her opposition to increasing France’s contribution to the EU budget could jeopardise EU-wide funding. Le Pen is threatening to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget, including a proposed €100bn facility for Ukraine. This is the mechanism through which the EU hopes to sustain Kyiv financially beyond 2028.
A Le Pen presidency could also give governments further from the frontline political cover to scale back their support. For Italy, Spain, Greece, Austria, Hungary and Slovakia, Ukraine is a lower priority and Italian support could weaken further after next year’s election.
The resulting bilateralisation of aid could leave a smaller group of northern and western European countries shouldering the burden. They would struggle to compensate for the loss of contributions from much of southern and central Europe .
Le Pen would also threaten Ukraine’s EU membership prospects and the bloc’s sanctions regime against Russia. Ukraine’s membership of the EU would become virtually impossible: key decisions require unanimity, and Le Pen has already opposed Kyiv’s accession . Nor would she be alone in her reluctance. Despite their public commitments, many EU governments harbour serious reservations about admitting Ukraine.
Sanctions would be equally vulnerable. Le Pen has advocated lifting EU sanctions on Russia since 2017. The bloc’s economic sanctions are due for renewal in July 2027, and a French veto could bring them to an end. She could also block the renewal of sanctions against individuals and veto any new packages.
In short, a Le Pen presidency could simultaneously undermine the three pillars of Europe’s support for Ukraine: on financing, EU membership and sanctions on Russia .
Let us imagine for a moment the worst-case scenario – as a result of Europe’s inability to sustain Ukraine after a Le Pen victory, Kyiv is pushed into a settlement on Moscow’s terms . Russia gets constitutional recognition of its annexation of Donetsk and Luhansk (and possibly even Zaporizhzhia and Kherson). Moscow also imposes political and security conditions on Kyiv: a prohibition on Nato membership, a cap on the size of its armed forces, and the political demands Moscow dresses up as “denazification”.
After an unprovoked invasion and almost five years of ruthless Russian attacks on civilians, Ukrainians would see the deal as a humiliating defeat. The humiliation would be greater still if Kyiv signed under pressure from Washington, with support from some parts of Europe and opposition from others.
Above all, the deal would be a humanitarian tragedy. Ceding the rest of the Donbas would leave tens of thousands of civilians under Russian occupation. They would face what occupation has meant elsewhere: mass detentions, forced disappearances and torture. Others, who manage to get evacuated, would add to Ukraine’s internally displaced population.
Because any transfer of territory requires a referendum, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would have to hold one and would probably put the whole deal on the ballot. Ukrainians would very likely reject it, opening an unprecedented political crisis. If Ukraine could no longer keep fighting, Zelenskyy would face two bad options: overrule the vote and impose a deeply unpopular deal; or resign and leave a vacuum for the next government to fill.
after newsletter promotion
Either way, protesters would probably fill the streets, opponents would challenge the agreement in court and whoever signed it would lose office. The deal would also need to clear parliament, where it could be voted down because few MPs would want their names on it. If it were instead imposed outside the constitution, politics would splinter into factions, some vowing to scrap the settlement and others insisting on moving on.
The economy is likely to follow. Donors and investors who had planned to fund reconstruction would pull back, leaving billions in potential deals on the table. The threat of Russia’s re-invasion and political instability would stall reconstruction. Millions more Ukrainians would then head west to rejoin their families, escaping a deal that fails to provide proper security guarantees and leaving economic devastation behind. At the same time, many soldiers would refuse to lay down their arms and keep up a guerrilla war in the ceded parts of Donbas. These units would be hard to rein in, possibly handing Moscow a pretext to resume full-scale fighting.
Over time, the sense of betrayal is bound to harden into resentment of western partners and Kyiv’s wartime elites alike. Most dangerous of all, Russia would probably use the pause to rebuild its economy and army. Soon, Vladimir Putin may feel tempted to exploit Ukraine’s chaos and invade again. The weak security framework of a deal on Russia’s terms would make this possible. Europe would be left with a broken, embittered and heavily armed state on its border, and an emboldened Russia behind it.
None of this is inevitable. Ukrainians have shown little appetite for capitulation, and weeks of US pressure have not shifted public opinion. Kyiv also understands that Moscow’s terms are probably designed to produce exactly this kind of turmoil. Ukraine would accept such a deal only if it had no other choice.
Getting there would necessitate a combination of things going wrong at the same time: a full US cut-off of intelligence and military support that lets Russia push the front back; European funding drying up with no bilateral substitute; and a Russian escalation backed by new mobilisation. Each is possible; together, they are unlikely. Nonetheless, this scenario should give EU capitals serious pause for thought. Policy should be built on the worst-case scenario rather than wishful thinking that Le Pen, in power, will moderate her view of Ukraine, in the way that Meloni has .
Ukraine’s outlook is bleaker than at any point since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Putin’s strategy has always been to outlast the west and achieve politically what he cannot secure on the battlefield. That prospect is becoming more plausible – not because Ukraine is losing the will to fight, or even because of Washington’s retreat, but because of what may happen in Europe next year, making it the weakest link in its own strategy to defeat Russia.
Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Grou

articles.title_orig: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.title_zh: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.
Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X.
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.
